subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a G3P1 obstetric history presents to your gynaecology emergency clinic with right-sided pelvic pain and light PV spotting for 24 hours. Her last menstrual period was 6+3 weeks ago. Two years ago she had a laparoscopic left salpingectomy for a ruptured left tubal ectopic. She and her partner have been actively trying to conceive for the past 8 months. She is haemodynamically stable and has no shoulder tip pain.

On examination she has right adnexal tenderness without peritonism. Her serum beta hCG is 3200 IU/L today, and a repeat 48 hours ago was 1900 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows an empty uterus with an endometrium of 12 mm, a 2.4 cm right tubal mass without foetal cardiac activity and a small amount of free pelvic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Full blood count and coagulation are within normal limits. She has no significant medical history and no allergies. Her body surface area is calculated at 1.75 m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right adnexal tenderness without peritonism; cervix closed on speculum; scant blood in vagina; no shoulder tip pain
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 3200 IU/L (today) rising from 1900 IU/L (48 hours ago); TVUS empty uterus, right tubal 2.4 cm mass no cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas free fluid; Hb 128 g/L (115-165); coagulation within normal limits; body surface area 1.75 m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Expectant management with beta hCG surveillance twice weekly aiming for spontaneous resolution over 2-4 weeks
options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling beta hCG and small mass; her beta hCG is rising which excludes this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area with day 4 and 7 beta hCG
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a reasonable option (mass under 3.5 cm, beta hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, no significant pain), but with the contralateral tube already lost, preserving fertility takes priority; conservative surgical salpingostomy is preferred over medical management here to allow future ipsilateral tubal function without waiting weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with careful haemostasis and post-operative beta hCG surveillance
options.rationale: With prior contralateral salpingectomy the right tube is her only tube; conservative salpingostomy preserves tubal patency while removing the ectopic and gives the best chance of future spontaneous conception. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy as definitive treatment given the ectopic in the sole remaining tube
options.rationale: Salpingectomy on the sole remaining tube commits her to IVF; salpingostomy preserves tubal function and is preferred if technically feasible in this context. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Ultrasound-guided intra-sac methotrexate injection under transvaginal guidance today
options.rationale: Direct sac injection is used for cornual or interstitial ectopic; standard tubal ectopic is managed medically with systemic methotrexate or surgically. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy include beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, reliable follow-up and no contraindications (renal or hepatic dysfunction, blood dyscrasia, breastfeeding, active pulmonary or peptic ulcer disease, immunodeficiency). Salpingectomy is preferred when the contralateral tube is healthy because recurrence risk after salpingostomy in the same tube is higher than a new ectopic in a normal contralateral tube. However, when the contralateral tube has already been removed or is grossly diseased, salpingostomy is preferred to preserve fertility. Methotrexate is an alternative when surgery is declined but has a longer resolution timeline and lower success in the setting.
key_points: Salpingectomy is preferred when contralateral tube is healthy.
Salpingostomy is preferred when contralateral tube is absent or diseased.
Methotrexate requires beta hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm and no cardiac activity.
Direct sac injection is reserved for cornual or interstitial ectopics.
explanation.pearls: Prior contralateral salpingectomy inverts the usual salpingectomy-vs-salpingostomy preference: preserve the only remaining tube with salpingostomy where technically feasible.

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 at 33+4 weeks gestation admitted overnight with hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg. Overnight she has developed severe headache resistant to paracetamol, epigastric pain and reduced urine output. She has had no seizures. Foetal movements are reduced. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 155/min with reduced variability but no decelerations.

Investigations show blood pressure 168/112 mmHg after two doses of intravenous labetalol 20 mg. Platelets are 82 x10^9/L (150-450), creatinine has risen from 62 micromol/L at booking to 118 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 148 U/L (<45), urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30). Urine output has been 25 mL/hour for the last 4 hours. She has had 1 g magnesium sulfate loading given 30 minutes ago. Her partner is at the bedside. Foetal biometry today shows growth on the 15th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, foetal HR 155/min
data_table.Examination: Alert but distressed, brisk deep tendon reflexes without clonus, right upper quadrant tenderness, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, symphysio-fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90) rising from 62; ALT 148 U/L (<45); urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30); urine output 25 mL/h for 4 hours; CTG baseline 155/min reduced variability

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue intravenous labetalol and reassess blood pressure and urine output in another 2 hours before deciding on delivery
options.rationale: She has severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic, haematologic); delaying delivery risks eclampsia, HELLP progression and abruption. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Give a further intravenous fluid bolus of 500 mL normal saline for oliguria and titrate the antihypertensive to target
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid loading in severe pre-eclampsia risks pulmonary oedema; oliguria in this context is expected and does not justify volume expansion. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Cease magnesium sulfate loading dose because platelets under 100 x10^9/L are a contraindication to magnesium
options.rationale: Platelets under 100 are not a contraindication to magnesium sulfate; magnesium reduces eclampsia risk and should continue. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Give first dose of antenatal corticosteroid and plan delivery within 24-48 hours after stabilising blood pressure
options.rationale: Delivery is the definitive treatment; the SOMANZ pathway for severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ dysfunction at 34 weeks or less is stabilise, give corticosteroid, and deliver within 24-48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Perform emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia without waiting for corticosteroid effect
options.rationale: Immediate delivery is reserved for eclampsia, uncontrollable severe hypertension, pulmonary oedema, foetal distress or placental abruption; stabilisation and steroid come first when possible. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with end-organ dysfunction (renal impairment, hepatic derangement, thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L, cerebral or visual disturbance, pulmonary oedema) at less than 34 weeks gestation warrants stabilisation, magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroid administration and planned delivery within 24-48 hours, provided foetal and maternal condition allow. Immediate delivery is indicated for eclampsia, uncontrollable hypertension despite maximal therapy, pulmonary oedema, non-reassuring foetal status, or placental abruption. Blood pressure target during labour is under 160/110 mmHg. Fluid restriction (80 mL/h) is preferred over aggressive resuscitation because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. Magnesium is continued for 24 hours post-delivery.
key_points: Delivery is definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia.
Severe pre-eclampsia at less than 34 weeks: steroid, stabilise, deliver in 24-48 hours.
Fluid restrict to 80 mL/h; avoid aggressive volume loading.
Continue magnesium for 24 hours post-delivery.
explanation.pearls: In severe pre-eclampsia under 34 weeks with end-organ involvement, deliver within 24-48 hours after antenatal corticosteroid; do not push fluids for oliguria as pulmonary oedema is the greater risk.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Guideline

stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your general practice for a routine cervical screening test. She has had one previous negative test at age 25. She has no post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding or vaginal discharge. She is up to date with HPV vaccination from a school program. She has a new male partner and uses combined oral contraception. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago.

The cervical screening test (CST) reports oncogenic HPV positive (non-16/18 types) with reflex liquid-based cytology showing possible low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pLSIL). Speculum examination at the time of collection showed a clinically normal cervix with no contact bleeding or visible lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Speculum: clinically normal cervix, no contact bleeding, no visible lesion
data_table.Investigations: CST oncogenic HPV positive (non-16/18); reflex LBC possible low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management according to the National Cervical Screening Program?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 6 months and refer to colposcopy only if oncogenic HPV persists at that visit
options.rationale: The 6-month follow-up applies to unsatisfactory or borderline categories; this is intermediate risk requiring 12-month HPV. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

options.text: Refer to colposcopy within 8 weeks because the reflex cytology reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
options.rationale: pLSIL with non-16/18 HPV is intermediate risk in the NCSP; direct colposcopy referral is triggered by HSIL, HPV 16 or 18, or symptomatic bleeding, not intermediate risk. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

options.text: Refer to gynaecology for LLETZ excision because possible LSIL requires immediate treatment to prevent progression
options.rationale: LLETZ is reserved for confirmed high-grade lesions at colposcopy; low-grade lesions are surveilled, not excised. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

options.text: Return to routine 5-yearly screening because HPV vaccination status makes progression to invasive cancer negligible
options.rationale: Vaccinated women still require screening as scheduled; a positive HPV result mandates the standard risk-stratified follow-up regardless of vaccination. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

options.text: Repeat oncogenic HPV test in 12 months and refer to colposcopy if oncogenic HPV persists at that repeat
options.rationale: Non-16/18 HPV with negative or low-grade cytology is intermediate risk in the NCSP; 12-month HPV recall is the standard pathway. (Source: NCSP Cervical Screening in Australia)

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP uses a primary HPV screening approach with reflex cytology on positive samples. Higher risk (HPV 16 or 18 detected, or intermediate risk with any HSIL cytology) triggers direct colposcopy referral. Intermediate risk (oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with negative, unsatisfactory, or low-grade cytology) triggers repeat HPV test in 12 months, with colposcopy if oncogenic HPV persists. Lower risk (HPV negative) returns to 5-yearly screening. Immediate colposcopy also applies to symptomatic bleeding, visible cervical lesion, or clinical suspicion regardless of screen result.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 detected: refer to colposcopy.
Non-16/18 with HSIL cytology: refer to colposcopy.
Non-16/18 with normal or low-grade cytology: repeat in 12 months.
Symptomatic bleeding or visible lesion: refer regardless of result.
explanation.pearls: Under the National Cervical Screening Program, non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with normal or low-grade cytology is intermediate risk: repeat HPV in 12 months.

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture recognition in VBAC labour
stem:
You are called to the birth suite for a 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 39+5 weeks gestation undergoing a planned vaginal birth after caesarean. Her previous caesarean two years ago was for breech at term with a low transverse incision and uncomplicated recovery. Her first birth was a normal vaginal delivery. Labour has been augmented with a low-dose oxytocin infusion for slow progress from 6 cm dilatation, and she has an epidural in situ. She is currently 8 cm dilated.

Continuous cardiotocography over the last 20 minutes shows late decelerations to 90/min with slow recovery. She reports a new severe suprapubic tearing pain between contractions that broke through her epidural, and there is a small amount of fresh vaginal bleeding. The presenting part is felt at station -1 on vaginal examination now, whereas 20 minutes ago it was at station 0. Her blood pressure has dropped from 118/72 to 92/58 mmHg over the last 10 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: New suprapubic tearing pain breaking through epidural; fresh PV bleeding; presenting part regressed from 0 to -1 station
data_table.Investigations: CTG late decelerations to 90/min with slow recovery; foetal baseline 165/min; oxytocin infusion running

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Cease oxytocin infusion and prepare for immediate category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: This clinical picture is diagnostic of uterine rupture; category 1 caesarean is the only life-saving intervention for mother and foetus. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Increase oxytocin infusion to strengthen contractions and re-examine in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Increasing oxytocin in a labouring VBAC with suspected rupture worsens tearing and foetal compromise; oxytocin should be ceased. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Give a further epidural bolus for pain and continue expectant management to full dilatation
options.rationale: Masking pain from uterine rupture and continuing labour risks maternal exsanguination and foetal death. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Apply a foetal scalp electrode and take a foetal blood sample to confirm distress before decision
options.rationale: The combination of maternal shock, tearing pain, PV bleeding and station regression is diagnostic; further tests would only delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

options.text: Attempt an assisted vaginal delivery with ventouse to expedite birth given cervical dilation of 8 cm
options.rationale: Ventouse requires full dilatation and does not address the ruptured uterus; only laparotomy can control haemorrhage and deliver the foetus safely. (Source: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture during VBAC is uncommon (0.3-0.7 percent) but catastrophic. Signs include abnormal cardiotocography (bradycardia in around 70 percent of cases is the earliest sign), maternal haemodynamic instability, severe suprapubic pain breaking through epidural, PV bleeding, loss of station of the presenting part, and cessation of previously effective contractions. Immediate management is cessation of oxytocin and category 1 caesarean section; delay increases perinatal and maternal mortality. Repair of the uterus at laparotomy may be possible but hysterectomy is required if bleeding cannot be controlled. Oxytocin augmentation in VBAC labour is associated with increased rupture risk and requires careful titration.
key_points: Loss of station plus tearing pain plus maternal shock is diagnostic of rupture.
Foetal bradycardia is the earliest and commonest CTG finding.
Cease oxytocin immediately and proceed to category 1 caesarean.
Oxytocin augmentation increases rupture risk in VBAC.
explanation.pearls: In VBAC labour, sudden loss of station of the presenting part with tearing pain breaking through the epidural and maternal shock is uterine rupture; call the category 1 caesarean immediately.

sources.label: RANZCOG Birth After Previous Caesarean Section Statement

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man 6 months after commencing olanzapine 10 mg nightly for a first episode of schizophrenia. He is stable on the current dose with resolved positive symptoms and returning to work part time. He has gained 8 kg since starting olanzapine and his current BMI is 27 kg/m2. He has no personal history of type 2 diabetes but his father was diagnosed at age 45. He smokes 10 cigarettes daily and eats a takeaway-heavy diet.

He has had a full baseline metabolic screen before starting olanzapine including weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting lipids, fasting glucose and prolactin. He now attends for routine follow up. He would like to continue olanzapine as it has clearly helped his symptoms and asks what monitoring he should have.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Weight 92 kg, waist circumference 98 cm, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Baseline (6 months ago): fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4 percent, total cholesterol 4.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L, prolactin 320 mIU/L (<430)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan for this patient?

options.text: Fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c annually; weight and blood pressure at each mental state review
options.rationale: Metabolic bloods including lipids and glucose are required at 3 and 12 months in the first year, then annually; annually alone underuses early detection. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Fasting lipids, glucose and HbA1c now and again at 12 months, then annually; weight and BP each visit
options.rationale: RANZCP schedule includes 3-month and 12-month metabolic bloods in year one then annually; 6-month timing captures the fast weight gain window for olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Cease olanzapine now and switch to aripiprazole because weight gain of over 5 kg mandates change
options.rationale: Switching is considered after ongoing metabolic derangement despite lifestyle intervention; a single 8 kg gain does not itself mandate a switch, especially in a well-responder. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Repeat only prolactin and ECG now, deferring metabolic bloods until 12 months post-initiation
options.rationale: Prolactin is not the main monitor for olanzapine (a low-prolactin agent); metabolic bloods are the priority in the first year. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for glucose tolerance test now regardless of the current fasting glucose result today
options.rationale: OGTT is not routine; fasting glucose and HbA1c are the RANZCP monitoring standards. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics cause weight gain, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia, most marked with olanzapine and clozapine. Baseline metabolic screen before starting includes weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting lipids, fasting glucose and HbA1c (plus prolactin if symptomatic). The recommended schedule is repeat at 3 months, at 6 months for high-risk agents, at 12 months, and annually thereafter, with weight and blood pressure at every visit. Persistent metabolic derangement despite lifestyle intervention triggers consideration of switching agent, adding metformin, or optimising cardiovascular risk factors.
key_points: Baseline metabolic screen before starting an antipsychotic.
Recheck at 3 months, 12 months in year 1, then annually.
High-risk agents (olanzapine, clozapine) warrant additional 6-month check.
Weight and BP at every visit; lifestyle counselling from initiation.
explanation.pearls: RANZCP metabolic monitoring for antipsychotics: fasting lipids, glucose, HbA1c at baseline, 3 months, 12 months and annually; add 6-month check for high-risk agents like olanzapine and clozapine.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for 5 years with excellent mood stability. She has had no manic or depressive relapses in that time. Her last set of monitoring bloods 12 months ago showed lithium level 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90) and calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60). She attends your outpatient clinic for routine review; she has no symptoms of toxicity, no polyuria and no cognitive concerns.

She takes no other medications, does not smoke and drinks no alcohol. She is on a stable diet with regular fluid intake. There is no personal or family history of thyroid disease. She would like to know what long-term monitoring is required from here on.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no cognitive impairment, no goitre, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 12 months ago: lithium 0.7 mmol/L; TSH 2.4 mIU/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; calcium 2.32 mmol/L; today's clinical review only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing monitoring plan?

options.text: Check lithium level annually; renal, thyroid and parathyroid function only if symptoms of derangement develop
options.rationale: Renal, thyroid and calcium monitoring is required at least 6-monthly on long-term lithium regardless of symptoms; symptom-based only under-monitors known adverse effects. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function tests every 3 months for the next year
options.rationale: 3-monthly is more frequent than required for stable long-term lithium; 6-monthly is the standard ongoing schedule. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Repeat lithium level, urea and electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function every 6 months as long as she remains stable
options.rationale: The RANZCP schedule for stable long-term lithium is lithium level plus renal, thyroid and calcium every 6 months once beyond the first year. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate to avoid further renal exposure risk in the coming years
options.rationale: Switching a well-responder to another agent risks relapse; monitoring is preferred as long as renal function remains stable. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

options.text: Add annual glomerular filtration rate estimate but omit thyroid function tests because she is asymptomatic
options.rationale: Thyroid function is checked at least every 6 months on lithium because hypothyroidism is often subclinical initially. (Source: RANZCP Lithium Long Term Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Lithium requires ongoing monitoring because of its narrow therapeutic index (0.4-1.0 mmol/L for maintenance) and known long-term risks: reduced glomerular filtration, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia. Schedule after initial titration and 12 months of stability is lithium level plus urea, creatinine, calcium and TSH every 6 months. Any change in dose, addition of interacting medications (thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs) or intercurrent illness (dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea) prompts an interim level. Signs of toxicity include tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures. Ensure adequate hydration and consistent salt intake.
key_points: 6-monthly lithium level plus renal, thyroid and calcium after year 1.
Interim level if dose change, intercurrent illness or new interacting drug.
Long-term risks include CKD, DI, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
Therapeutic range for maintenance is 0.4-1.0 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: Long-term lithium monitoring: lithium level plus urea, creatinine, calcium and TSH every 6 months once stable, with an interim level for any intercurrent illness or new interacting drug.
